output.summary: Kevin Kelly argues that a creator does not need millions of fans or a blockbuster hit to make a living; roughly 1,000 'true fans', people who will buy anything the creator makes, can suffice. If each true fan spends about $100 a year (one day's wages) and pays the creator directly, that yields about $100,000 a year. He says the web and long-tail dynamics make such fans findable and directly reachable, while the long tail on its own gives creators little. He offers this as a saner alternative to stardom or poverty, with caveats about team size, intermediaries, and the work of tending fans. The essay is an updated 2016-era version of a 2008 original, which adds the idea's history, examples and early crowdfunding models.
main_claims: A creator can make a living with about 1,000 true fans, defined as fans who will buy anything the creator produces, rather than needing millions of customers or a hit.
The math rests on two conditions: earning about $100 profit per true fan per year, and a direct relationship so the creator keeps the full payment instead of a small share going to intermediaries.

The number 1,000 is a rough order of magnitude that must be adjusted for per-fan revenue, living costs, team size, and the use of intermediaries or helpers; the true number can only be found by trying.

The web and the long tail make niche audiences reachable (any one-in-a-million appeal can find 1,000 fans), but the long tail alone mostly benefits aggregators and consumers, not creators, so creators need direct true-fan relationships to escape it.
Fans can lift a creator beyond their raw numbers by spending more per person, paying directly, and enabling new support models such as micro-patronage, pre-financing and crowdfunding.
True fans offer an alternative path between poverty and stardom, but cultivating them is time-consuming and not suited to everyone, and can be combined with traditional intermediaries.
background: Basic profit and income arithmetic (revenue per customer times number of customers)
The role of intermediaries in creative industries (publishers, record labels, studios, retailers)
The Long Tail idea (Chris Anderson): sales distribution with a few bestsellers and many low-selling items
Peer-to-peer web, online retail aggregators such as Amazon and Netflix
Crowdfunding platforms such as Kickstarter and Patreon

sections.label: core-idea
sections.title: The core idea: what a true fan is and why 1,000 suffice
key_points: A true fan will buy anything you produce, such as traveling far to see you, buying every format of a work, or buying a product sight unseen.
Success as a living, not a fortune, needs only thousands of true fans rather than millions of customers.
A thousand is feasible: you might remember all their names, and adding one a day takes only a few years.

sections.label: the-math
sections.title: The math and its two criteria
key_points: Criterion one: earn about $100 profit per true fan per year, equivalent to one day's wages, which pushes creators to offer existing fans more.
Criterion two: a direct relationship so the creator keeps the full payment, giving $100 times 1,000 = $100,000 a year.
The figure is adjustable: $50 per fan needs 2,000 fans, $200 needs 500, lower living costs need fewer.
Original 2008 version states the same one-day-wage assumption and notes that the truest fans spend far more than the average.

sections.label: adjustments-and-caveats
sections.title: Adjusting the formula: teams, intermediaries, media and regular fans
key_points: Teams need proportionally more fans (33% more people means 33% more fans, linear rather than exponential growth).
Not every creator wants to deal with fans; a helper or manager raises the number of fans needed, and handing the job to middlemen is usually worse.
Indirect income, such as blogging via ads or books via publishers, inflates the needed number of fans but not to blockbuster levels.
The number varies by medium and place (e.g. 500 for a painter, 5,000 for a video maker in the 2008 essay) and can only be found by trying; Kelly allows it could be off by an order of magnitude.
Regular fans surround true fans in concentric circles, perhaps adding about 50% income, and true fans act as marketers for them.

sections.label: why-now
sections.title: Why it is newly possible: direct relationships and the long tail
key_points: Last-century intermediaries meant creators lacked direct contact, even customers' names, so they needed much larger audiences.
Peer-to-peer communication and payment let creators sell directly worldwide and keep the full payment, which reduces the fans needed.
In the web's network the obscure item is one click from the bestseller; aggregators found the tail's total sales rival the head's and built recommendation engines and search to surface obscure items.
A one-in-a-million appeal among billions of people still yields thousands of potential fans; big corporations are ill suited to serve niches, leaving the tail open to creators.
The original essay argues the long tail is a mixed blessing for creators (more competition, downward price pressure, little sales gain), which motivates the true-fan path.

sections.label: history-and-models
sections.title: Precedents and models of fan support
key_points: Related ideas from the 2008 essay: microcelebrity (Carl Steadman's 1,500 people), micro-patronage, and the Street Performer Protocol of Kelsey and Schneier.

Examples: Lawrence Watt-Evans funding a novel by fan donations and getting by on an estimated 200 true fans alongside traditional publishing; Greg Stolze's pre-financed games; Jill Sobule's fan-funded album with tiered pledges.
Fundable's all-or-nothing model, illustrated by Amelia's pre-sold CD, protects backers.
Fans help beyond their numbers by buying more each, spending directly, and enabling new support models.

sections.label: crowdfunding
sections.title: Crowdfunding as a tool for true-fan creators
key_points: Roughly 2,000 crowdfunding platforms exist with different models: all-or-nothing, partial funding, completed projects, ongoing projects like Patreon.
Kickstarter's average successful project has 241 funders, far below 1,000, so 1,000 true fans could in principle fund a campaign, though success depends on what you ask.

sections.label: costs-and-takeaway
sections.title: Costs, combining paths, and the takeaway
key_points: Cultivating fans is time-consuming, sometimes nerve-racking, and can become another full-time job or a demanding part-time task.
The approach is not exclusive: Kelly uses big publishers, self-publishing and Kickstarter, with true fans enriching each route.

Takeaway: an alternative to stardom, and the usual alternative to it is poverty (Towse's 1995 survey of British artists found average earnings below subsistence); a saner destination that one is more likely to reach.
Updates link to follow-up pieces including a critical survey, which signals the claim is contested; the document itself gives little evidence beyond anecdotes and stated assumptions.
